name: Nikhil Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and this conversation is confidential. What does a usual workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I fit the finishing parts of school buildings: doors, frames, skirting and ironmongery. My trade certificate got me into carpentry, and now I know a good fire door by the way it closes. I like seeing a classroom ready before the children arrive.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is harder than it used to be?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Stairs and paperwork. Sanna, my partner, works at the library; our grown children are out on their own, and we have about four months saved. I am fifty eight and do not use AI tools. We are discussing retirement, but we have not fixed a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the tea-break crowd the school doors still need someone to fit and check them. If the office saves an hour on paperwork, fine; I will keep my pencil and level.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sanna and I have about four months of expenses put by, and our grown children are living on their own. My carpenter rate is ordinary and a few local builders take similar work, so I can see a path to the retirement date we have discussed if my knees hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep fitting doors on the school extension and checking the fire-door gaps with a gauge. I would keep the same household savings transfer, rather than buy a tool I have never needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The stairs still wear me out, but my pay is steady enough for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the gap gauge for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wide fire-door gap is still a gap however neat the office form looks. I mark any bad frame for refitting before the room opens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Will you try an AI tool for forms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have never used one, and the site clerk can send the forms while I measure the door.

say: I would tell colleagues **school fire doors** still need hands-on fitting and checks.
I would accept a small **office saving** without changing my own tools.
think: Our **four-month reserve** and grown children make current bills manageable.
My **knees** may limit the last years of work more than a plateau does.
do: Keep fitting **school doors** and checking fire-door gaps with a gauge.
Maintain the existing **savings transfer** at its current amount.
feel: **Calm** about pay, with familiar concern about aching knees.
S0.quote: A wide fire-door gap is still a gap however neat the office form looks.
fieldNote: His current income and moderate savings support a **calm plateau** despite ordinary project gaps.
He has never used AI and would continue the **existing fitting routine**.

steps.text: Keep fitting school fire doors and checking gaps with a gauge

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the office can book hinges faster, but it should not send a crew to fit a door that has not arrived. I would ask for a printed schedule signed by someone who has seen the delivery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planners may be fewer, and the contractor could squeeze paid days between school jobs. I might lose some hours before the next site begins, though Sanna’s library wage and our savings could bridge a short gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the next two monthly rosters with my pay slips and ask the site manager who signs the new schedule. If paid days fall, Sanna and I would put off replacing the sitting-room sofa until the next contract starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a real pay gap, not about learning an app. A sofa can wait; a household bill cannot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would convince you the schedule is right?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A delivery note, the correct hinge size and a named person at the store. I do not want to carry a heavy door up stairs twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Sanna need to add shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. Her library wage already helps, and I would wait for actual lost days before asking her to change hours.

say: I would ask for a **signed delivery schedule** before moving heavy school doors.
I would keep a **hinge-size check** on every delivery.
think: Paid days **between contracts** could shrink under faster planning.
Sanna’s **library pay** and our savings can cover a short gap.
do: Compare the next **two rosters** against pay slips for lost days.
Delay the **sitting-room sofa** only if paid days fall.
S1.quote: A sofa can wait; a household bill cannot.
fieldNote: His concern is a **realistic wage gap**, even while AI only plans the job.
He would delay furniture after **measured lost days**, keeping mortgage payments first.

steps.text: Delay sitting-room sofa only after two rosters show fewer paid days

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the school crew that thinking AI in 2028 can make plans, but a robot will not fit a fire door until around 2031. The contractor should test one in an empty room with the equipment isolated first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty three when capable robots arrive, and Sanna and I had been thinking of finishing work later than that if my knees permit. A loss of fitting days before we have enough saved could force us to use the reserve, though there are some other carpentry sites nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid door-fitting shifts and ask the contractor for its written staffing dates. If two rosters cut my hours, I would apply to posted local finishing jobs and leave only for a firm wage that covers our remaining housing costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I still have choices. Four months of savings cannot replace years of the door-fitting wages our household may still need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire as soon as robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Checking whether we could afford to stop is only preparation. I will keep working while the pay and my knees allow it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is an isolated test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Power off while the crew marks where nobody may stand, then a supervised restart in an empty room. I would not test a moving arm beside children in a school.

say: Thinking AI in **2028** changes plans before 2031 robots fit school doors.
I would require an **isolated empty-room test** before any robot works near pupils.
think: At **sixty three**, I may still need door-fitting wages when capable robots arrive.
Four months saved and **some local sites** help, but cannot fund years without work.
do: Keep **paid school fitting** shifts while offered.
Apply to **posted local finishing jobs** after two reduced rosters only for housing-covering firm pay.
feel: **Anxious** about possible lost days before an affordable retirement.
S2.quote: Four months of savings cannot replace years of the door-fitting wages our household may still need.
fieldNote: He expects a possible **income gap**, but does not claim an immediate job loss.
The search requires **posted work** and firm pay after two reduced rosters.

steps.text: Keep paid school door-fitting shifts while contractor work exists
Apply to posted local finishing jobs after two reduced rosters for firm housing-covering pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years lets us find out whether a robot can fit a crooked school door without scraping its frame. The builder should pay a joiner to check the result.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2031 may rewrite job sheets, which the clerk can handle. Hands-on robots arrive around 2034 when I would be sixty six; Sanna and I might have stopped regular work by then if our accounts and health allow, but that is not certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep fitting doors next year and ask Sanna to review our household figures every autumn. If the contractor offers a paid inspection post with a posted wage that suits us, I would consider applying; I would not buy a robot course for a job no one has advertised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the trade, less worried about my next wages than in the fast case. The extra years may be enough to finish on our own terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you bring retirement forward because of 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We are still working out an affordable date, and the robot date does not pay the bills. I will not resign based on a projection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the paid inspector check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fire-door gap, closing force and fastening into the frame. A photograph cannot tell me a fire door closes safely. The inspector needs authority to reject a bad fitting.

say: I would ask for **paid human inspection** of any 2034 robot-fitted school door.
I would keep **fire-door checks** on the finished frame rather than accept a photo.
think: I may have stopped regular work before **2034** if health and accounts support it.
The **2031 job sheets** change before robots reach the physical fitting work.
do: Keep **school door work** next year while paid shifts remain.
Review **retirement figures** with Sanna each autumn before choosing a date.
feel: **Uneasy** about future work while current wages appear stable.
S3.quote: A photograph cannot tell me a fire door closes safely.
fieldNote: He asks about affordable retirement without making an **early-exit decision**.
The possible inspection post is **not an offer**, so no actual job-change action is inferred here.

steps.text: Keep fitting school doors next year while paid shifts remain

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell younger joiners that a decade is enough to learn how a proper fire door feels before thinking AI in 2036 and robots around 2039. They should get real doors to fit, not just a video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty eight at the thinking date and seventy one when capable robots arrive. If Sanna and I can afford our planned retirement before 2036, the machines would reach the site after I leave; if not, I might still need shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep fitting school doors during 2026 and check the accounts with Sanna after each year of paid work. In the first year after 2036, if retired as planned, I would stay out of the site rota; if still employed, I would take only paid door shifts my knees can manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the machine timetable, with some concern about whether our accounts will stretch far enough. The longer gap lets me teach a younger fitter before I put down the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop earlier because of this card?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Sanna and I will stop when the household income and my health make it possible. A robot arriving in 2039 does not change the date by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you teach the younger fitter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Run a hand along the closing edge and measure the gap after the frame settles. A door that sticks today will not improve because the paperwork is neat.

say: I would protect **hands-on fitting** for younger joiners before 2036 thinking AI and 2039 robots.
I would explain **door-gap checks** after a frame settles.
think: I expect retirement before **2036** only if Sanna and I can fund it.
If still working after 2036, I would need **paid manageable shifts**, not a guaranteed pension.
do: Keep **2026 school fitting** shifts and review accounts annually.
After **2036**, take only manageable paid shifts if still employed.
feel: **Uneasy** about funding retirement, though distant robots do not threaten near-term wages.
S4.quote: A door that sticks today will not improve because the paperwork is neat.
fieldNote: He separates definite **2026 work** from employment after 2036, conditional on retirement funding.
The future robot date does not trigger **early retirement** or an assumed pension payment.

steps.text: Keep paid school door fitting during 2026 while knees allow
Take paid manageable door shifts after 2036 only if still employed; otherwise remain retired

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robots could take door-fitting days around 2031 before Sanna and I know we can afford to stop. A written staffing plan, firm local finishing jobs and clear household figures would help me decide.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks a school fire door after a robot fits it. A child needs the door to work when smoke is real, not only in a test room.

headlineQuote: A child needs the door to work when smoke is real, not only in a test room.
portrait: **Nikhil**, 58, is an experienced school-door fitter with a trade certificate, ordinary pay and four months of savings.
Sanna’s **library wage** helps, their children are grown, and some other carpentry sites are within reach.
He avoids **AI tools**, trusts physical door checks and treats retirement as an affordability decision rather than a machine date.
The **2028 case** worries him because 2031 robots may cut paid fitting days before he can stop working.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could reduce door-fitting days before he can afford retirement.
whatWouldHelp: A written **staffing plan**, firm local work and household figures would help him choose.
